strengths: Addresses an underexplored direction (training-free spatial acceleration) for DiT inference, complementing the more heavily studied temporal acceleration/caching literature.

Clear identification and diagnosis of two distinct artifact types (aliasing near edges, noise-timestep mismatch) caused by latent upsampling, with intuitive visualizations (Fig. 2, Fig. 4) that motivate the method design.

The noise-timestep rescheduling derivation (NT-DM) is grounded in a principled analysis of how upsampling changes the covariance structure of the flow-matching trajectory, and the distribution-matching formulation for adapting timestep schedules in a training-free setting is a reasonable technical contribution beyond simply reusing pyramidal-flow-style correlated noise injection.

Strong empirical results across two backbones (FLUX.1-dev, SD3) and multiple speedup regimes, with consistent improvements over relevant baselines (ToCa, RAS, Bottleneck Sampling) on FID, NIQE, CLIP-IQA, and compositional alignment metrics (T2I-CompBench, GenEval).
Demonstrated compatibility with caching-based temporal acceleration, showing additive speedups (up to ~7.9x) with modest quality loss, supporting the claimed complementarity.

Extensive appendix material: derivations, ablations (upsampling ratio, NT-DM component ablation), FLOPs breakdown for the extra VAE decode, and large uncurated qualitative galleries, which aids reproducibility and mitigates cherry-picking concerns.
weaknesses: The edge-region selection mechanism (Canny edge detection + top-k patch selection via one extra VAE decode) is a fairly simple heuristic; its sensitivity to the top-k ratio, image content, or failure cases (e.g., few edges, textured whole-image content) is not deeply analyzed, and the ablation in Fig. 6 uses only 3 prompts/ratios.

Results are limited to text-to-image generation on two flow-matching backbones (FLUX, SD3); no video diffusion or other DiT architectures are tested despite the framework being motivated as generally applicable to DiTs, and the authors themselves flag NT-DM as unverified beyond flow matching (Limitations section).

GenEval scores for RALU are sometimes noticeably lower than the base full-step model and occasionally lower than Bottleneck Sampling (e.g., Table 1, FLUX 4x: 0.639 vs 0.669 for Bottleneck; 7x: 0.646 vs 0.649), suggesting text-alignment gains are not uniformly superior, which is somewhat underdiscussed in the text that otherwise emphasizes RALU's superiority.

Key hyperparameters (stage timesteps e_k, s_k, top-k ratio, number of stages/steps per stage) appear to be manually chosen per model/speedup setting (Table S1, appendix B.2-style configs) rather than derived automatically, raising questions about the effort needed to tune RALU for new models or resolutions, which is not fully addressed as a limitation.

The paper compares to only one prior spatial-acceleration baseline (Bottleneck Sampling) since it claims to be the only other training-free spatial method; broader comparison against training-based cascaded/relay diffusion approaches (even as an upper-bound reference) is missing, making it harder to judge the absolute quality gap versus training-based multi-resolution methods.

Some experimental details (e.g., exact latency measurement protocol, whether TFLOPs include the extra VAE decode and Canny detection overhead consistently, batch size, hardware warm-up) could be more explicit to ensure fair reproducibility of the reported speedups.

strengths: Addresses an underexplored angle in DiT acceleration: training-free spatial acceleration via latent upsampling, which is complementary to the more heavily studied temporal (caching/forecasting) acceleration methods.

Clear diagnostic analysis (Sec. 3) that carefully identifies and empirically characterizes two distinct artifact types (aliasing from late upsampling, and distribution mismatch from noise injection), motivating the proposed design in a principled way rather than an ad hoc engineering fix.

The mixed-resolution/region-adaptive upsampling idea (only upsampling edge-prone regions early, keeping the rest low-res) is a sensible and reasonably novel way to trade off computation against artifact suppression, backed by an interpretable mechanism (Canny edge detection on Tweedie-estimated x0).

Noise-Timestep Matching (NT-Matching) is derived with an explicit closed-form analysis (matching first/second moments of the upsampled and target trajectory distributions, then minimizing JSD to fit a parametric timestep schedule), giving the method a level of mathematical grounding beyond typical heuristic noise-reinjection.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: two different base models (FLUX.1-dev, SD3), multiple standard metrics (ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, NIQE, T2I-CompBench, GenEval), comparisons to several temporal baselines and the only known spatial competitor (Bottleneck Sampling), plus integration experiments showing complementarity with temporal caching methods and timestep-distilled models (up to 15.9x speedup).

Thorough ablations (edge-detection method, fixed vs adaptive ratio, upsampling interpolation kernel, effect of NT-Matching via controlled JSD sweep) and artifact-ratio vs FLOPs comparison (Fig. 7) that directly supports the core claim of reduced artifacts at matched compute.
Appendices include GPU cross-hardware latency/memory results, detailed derivations, and large uncurated qualitative galleries, aiding reproducibility and reducing cherry-picking concerns.
weaknesses: Quantitative gains, while consistently favorable, are often modest in absolute metric terms (e.g., ImageReward 0.999 vs 0.972-0.992 for baselines at 7x on FLUX), and some competing methods win on individual metrics (e.g., RAS's GenEval/T2I-Comp at SD3 2x, TaylorSeer's NIQE in some settings), so the overall superiority rests on aggregate/qualitative judgment more than a uniform sweep.

The method introduces several hand-tuned hyperparameters (edge-ratio r, per-model {N_k}, {e_k}, shifting parameters h_k, c) that are separately fit per model/speedup setting (Table S1), raising questions about how much manual tuning transfers to new models/resolutions not tested (e.g., no results on video DiTs or other architectures despite the framing around DiTs broadly).

NT-Matching is explicitly stated in the Limitations to be tailored to flow-matching architectures, and the method's generality to other diffusion formulations (e.g., DDPM/U-Net, or non-rectified-flow DiTs) is untested, narrowing the claimed scope of 'DiTs' acceleration.

The perceptual/quality evaluation relies heavily on learned proxy metrics (ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, NIQE) without any human study, despite the paper's central claims being about visually perceptible artifacts (aliasing, mismatching); a small human preference study would strengthen the artifact-reduction claims considerably.

The three-stage pipeline (low-res denoise, edge-region early upsampling, full-resolution refinement) adds implementation complexity (Tweedie estimation, VAE decode, Canny edge detection, mask construction, JSD-based schedule fitting) relative to simpler baselines like TeaCache/TaylorSeer, and the runtime accounting of these auxiliary steps (edge detection ~2.48 TFLOPs) is only partially transparent for all settings.

Discussion section is largely speculative (open question about attention behavior across resolutions) rather than offering deeper insight, and the observed 'robustness' claim about token merging is only loosely connected via a brief pointer to unrelated work.

strengths: Identifies and clearly analyzes two distinct failure modes of naive latent upsampling for DiT spatial acceleration—aliasing artifacts in high-frequency edge regions and distribution-mismatching artifacts from noise/timestep discrepancies—supported by controlled empirical studies (Fig. 2, 3) that motivate the proposed design.

The proposed RALU method is principled: mixed-resolution/region-adaptive upsampling restricted to artifact-prone edge regions, combined with a mathematically derived Noise-Timestep Matching (NT-Matching) scheme that analytically aligns the post-upsampling distribution with the pretrained model's original timestep schedule; derivations are provided in detail in the appendix.

Strong empirical results across two base models (FLUX.1-dev, SD3) and multiple metrics (ImageReward, CLIP-IQA, NIQE, T2I-CompBench, GenEval), showing RALU consistently outperforms both temporal acceleration baselines and the only prior training-free spatial baseline (Bottleneck Sampling) at comparable FLOPs, achieving up to 7x speedup with minimal degradation.

Demonstrated complementarity with existing temporal acceleration methods and timestep-distilled models, reaching up to 15.9x combined speedup with limited quality loss, indicating practical value and broad applicability.

Thorough ablation studies (edge detection method, fixed vs. adaptive upsampling ratio, choice of upsampler, effect of NT-Matching via JSD) and inclusion of uncurated qualitative samples (Figs. S10-S13) strengthen credibility and reduce concern about cherry-picking.

Method is training-free, which is practically appealing compared to distillation or retraining-based acceleration approaches, and latency/FLOPs/VRAM are reported across two GPU types for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted to two flow-matching-based DiT backbones (FLUX.1-dev and SD3) at a single output resolution (1024x1024); generality of the approach (particularly NT-Matching, which is explicitly tailored to flow-matching schedules) to non-flow-matching diffusion formulations (e.g., DDPM/U-Net) or to higher-resolution generation regimes is unverified, a limitation the authors themselves acknowledge.

The method requires per-setting calibration: the edge-region ratio r and NT-Matching parameters (shifting parameters, noise correlation coefficient) are determined via numerical JSD minimization tuned separately for each model/speedup configuration (Table S1), which adds practical overhead when adapting to new acceleration targets not explicitly quantified in wall-clock terms.

Comparisons to genuine training-free spatial acceleration baselines are limited to a single prior method (Bottleneck Sampling); broader spatial-acceleration literature comparisons (if any exist) are not discussed beyond related work citations.

Quality assessment relies solely on automatic metrics and qualitative visual comparisons; no human preference/user study is included to corroborate the automatic metric improvements, despite artifacts being a primarily perceptual phenomenon.

Some presentation aspects (e.g., dense derivations in Sec. 4.2, notation overload with multiple subscripted parameters) could be streamlined for clarity, and the interaction between region-adaptive early upsampling and self-attention across mixed resolutions is left as an open question in the Discussion rather than being analyzed.
